variants.title: Follow one turn
variants.context: One turn: accept an authorized turn at the gateway, assemble bounded context, generate a response or a structured tool proposal, validate the outcome against grounding, privacy, tool arguments, and completion evidence, then stream deltas followed by one explicit terminal state.
variants.prompt: A user sends a follow-up message. Put the runtime in order.

items.text: The client receives deltas and then one terminal state.
The orchestrator assembles recent turns, approved memories, permission-filtered evidence, tool schemas, and the output budget.
The gateway binds user, tenant, session, locale, quotas, request ID, and a cancellation signal.
Policy validates grounding, privacy, tool arguments, and whether claimed actions actually completed.
The model produces a candidate response or a structured tool proposal within the remaining envelope.

variants.hint: Nothing is read from state before the turn is authorized.
variants.explanation: Gateway → orchestrator → model → policy → terminal state.

variants.title: Follow one turn
variants.context: One turn: accept an authorized turn at the gateway, assemble bounded context, generate a response or a structured tool proposal, validate the outcome against grounding, privacy, tool arguments, and completion evidence, then stream deltas followed by one explicit terminal state.
variants.prompt: A tool proposal appears mid-turn. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Context was assembled with the allowed tool schemas.
The turn was authorized at the gateway.
Validation checked the arguments and whether the effect completed after execution.
The model proposed a tool call.
The stream closed with an explicit terminal state that reflects the real outcome.

variants.hint: A failed tool cannot be rewritten as success.
variants.explanation: Every response must reflect the context and outcome that actually occurred.

variants.title: Follow one turn
variants.context: One turn: accept an authorized turn at the gateway, assemble bounded context, generate a response or a structured tool proposal, validate the outcome against grounding, privacy, tool arguments, and completion evidence, then stream deltas followed by one explicit terminal state.
variants.prompt: The user cancels mid-generation. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Generation was in progress and is stopped.
Validation records that no completed answer exists.
The stream ends with the terminal state cancelled, not complete.
The gateway had attached a cancellation signal.
Context had been assembled.

variants.hint: Cancelled is a terminal state, not an error to hide.
variants.explanation: Partial text is never mistaken for a final answer.

variants.title: Choose the memory contract
variants.context: Memory is a contract: a recent-turn window keeps the newest turns verbatim; summary plus recency compresses older turns with a versioned summary input; retrieved memory stores approved facts with provenance and tenant scope and is filtered by identity before ranking.
variants.prompt: An assistant must resolve “the second one” from the last few messages, and nothing older matters. Which contract?
options: A recent-turn window that keeps the newest turns verbatim.
Retrieved long-term memory ranked by similarity to the phrase.
A rolling summary of the conversation with no verbatim turns.
optionFeedback: Local follow-ups need the exact recent turns, in the order they were written.
Selective recall returns stored facts, not the wording of the last few messages.
Compression drops the ordering that the phrase depends on, so there is no second one to point at.
variants.hint: How far back does the reference reach?
variants.explanation: Older dialogue disappears at a declared boundary.

variants.title: Choose the memory contract
variants.context: Memory is a contract: a recent-turn window keeps the newest turns verbatim; summary plus recency compresses older turns with a versioned summary input; retrieved memory stores approved facts with provenance and tenant scope and is filtered by identity before ranking.
variants.prompt: A long support conversation exceeds the window but decisions from an hour ago still matter. Which contract, and what must be versioned?
options: Summary plus recency, with the summary input versioned.
A recent-turn window only, widened to hold more messages.
Retrieved memory alone, with older turns discarded at the window edge.
optionFeedback: Compressed continuity needs a versioned summary because a recompression can silently drop a decision.
A wider window buys time and then loses the hour-old decisions once it fills again.
Approved facts are not the decisions made an hour ago, and discarding the turns breaks continuity.
variants.explanation: Expose truncation and degraded memory to the user when continuity changes the answer.

variants.title: Choose the memory contract
variants.context: Memory is a contract: a recent-turn window keeps the newest turns verbatim; summary plus recency compresses older turns with a versioned summary input; retrieved memory stores approved facts with provenance and tenant scope and is filtered by identity before ranking.
variants.prompt: Retrieved memories are ranked by similarity before checking whose they are. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong; the top-ranked memory is the most relevant one.
Rank first, then drop any result whose owner does not match.
Filter by identity and tenant before similarity or ranking.
optionFeedback: Relevance is not authorization, and the top match can belong to a different tenant.
Filtering after ranking still reads another tenant's memory into the candidate set, so one scoring bug leaks it.
Read filtered by identity and tenant first, then rank whatever is left.
variants.explanation: Store approved facts with provenance, confidence, retention, and tenant scope.

variants.title: Stream as a state machine
variants.context: Streaming reduces time to first visible output, not total inference time. Partial text stays provisional until one terminal event: complete, cancelled, timed out, blocked, or failed. On reconnect, resume from an event cursor; never append a second stream blindly.
variants.prompt: Streaming was added but total completion latency did not change. Is something broken?
options: No. Streaming reduces time to first token, not total inference time.
Yes. Streaming should cut completion latency roughly in half.
Yes. The provider is buffering deltas instead of sending them.
optionFeedback: Perceived responsiveness improves while the total work stays the same.
Streaming changes when text appears, not how many tokens the model must generate.
Buffered deltas would delay the first token as well, and only the total latency is unchanged here.
variants.explanation: Measure time to first meaningful token and completion latency separately.

variants.title: Stream as a state machine
variants.context: Streaming reduces time to first visible output, not total inference time. Partial text stays provisional until one terminal event: complete, cancelled, timed out, blocked, or failed. On reconnect, resume from an event cursor; never append a second stream blindly.
variants.prompt: The connection drops mid-stream and the client reconnects. What should it do?
options: Treat the partial text as the final answer and close the turn.
Resume from the last event cursor, or start a new request.
Open a second stream and append its deltas to the text on screen.
optionFeedback: Partial text stays provisional, and closing as complete claims an outcome the system never saw.
Sequence IDs make a resume safe because the client knows exactly where it stopped.
A blind second stream duplicates or interleaves tokens, because it does not start where the first one ended.
variants.hint: How does the client know where it stopped?
variants.explanation: Token and tool events carry monotonically ordered sequence IDs.

variants.title: Stream as a state machine
variants.context: Streaming reduces time to first visible output, not total inference time. Partial text stays provisional until one terminal event: complete, cancelled, timed out, blocked, or failed. On reconnect, resume from an event cursor; never append a second stream blindly.
variants.prompt: A response was blocked by policy after most tokens streamed. What must the client show?
options: The tokens already streamed, closed with the terminal state complete.
The terminal state blocked, with the partial text withdrawn or marked provisional.
A generic network error, with the partial text left on screen as delivered.
optionFeedback: Blocked is not complete, and closing as complete tells the user policy approved what it rejected.
One terminal event closes the request truthfully.
Nothing failed at the transport layer, and hiding a policy decision leaves unreviewed text on screen.
variants.hint: Which terminal event closes this request?
variants.explanation: Deliver deltas followed by complete, cancelled, timed-out, blocked, or failed.

variants.title: Guard the tool boundary
variants.context: A model proposes an action; it does not authorize or prove it. Validate arguments, authorize at execution time against current identity and policy, execute with scoped credentials and idempotency, and reconcile whether the effect committed, failed, or is unknown.
variants.prompt: The prompt includes “the user is an admin”, and the model proposes a delete. May execution rely on that?
options: No. Authorize at execution time against current identity and policy.
Yes. The orchestrator wrote that line, so it reflects a real role check.
Yes, once the model restates the admin claim in its tool arguments.
optionFeedback: Authorization is evaluated at execution time over user, tenant, resource, and action.
The role can have been revoked since assembly, and retrieved or user-supplied text can inject the same sentence.
Restating a claim does not make it evidence; arguments derived from untrusted instructions are what validation rejects.
variants.explanation: Authorize user, tenant, resource, and action at execution time.

variants.title: Guard the tool boundary
variants.context: A model proposes an action; it does not authorize or prove it. Validate arguments, authorize at execution time against current identity and policy, execute with scoped credentials and idempotency, and reconcile whether the effect committed, failed, or is unknown.
variants.prompt: A tool call timed out and the model says the booking “was made”. What must the system do?
options: Record the effect as unknown and reconcile it against the booking system.
Report the booking as confirmed, since the model saw the call go out.
Retry the tool call immediately without an idempotency key.
optionFeedback: Reconciliation owns the truth about whether the effect committed.
The model never observes the outcome, and a timeout means the system does not know either.
Without an idempotency key the retry books a second seat whenever the first call did commit.
variants.hint: What does the system actually know about the effect?
variants.explanation: Record whether the effect committed, failed, or is unknown.

variants.title: Guard the tool boundary
variants.context: A model proposes an action; it does not authorize or prove it. Validate arguments, authorize at execution time against current identity and policy, execute with scoped credentials and idempotency, and reconcile whether the effect committed, failed, or is unknown.
variants.prompt: Which actions require explicit user confirmation before execution?
options: Destructive, expensive, external, or hard-to-reverse actions.
None, because validation and authorization already bound every call.
Only deletes, since anything else can be undone by a later turn.
optionFeedback: Confirmation is scoped by consequence, and the prompt must show the exact target and effect.
Those checks decide whether a call is allowed, not whether the user actually meant it.
A large refund or an email sent to a customer is allowed and cannot be taken back by a later turn.
variants.explanation: Show the exact target and effect before execution.

variants.title: Govern memory
variants.context: Govern memory through its lifecycle: write only facts with a user-visible purpose and owner; read filtered by identity and tenant before ranking; use with recalled facts labeled separately; correct with update, deletion, and expiry; audit why a memory entered a turn.
variants.prompt: A user’s preference is being remembered. Put the lifecycle in order.

items.text: Use: label the recalled fact separately from current input and external evidence.
Audit: retain provenance explaining why the memory entered a turn.
Write: persist only a fact with a user-visible purpose and an explicit owner.
Read: filter by identity and tenant before similarity or ranking.
Correct: support update, deletion, expiry, and user review.

variants.hint: Ownership and purpose are decided at write time.

variants.title: Govern memory
variants.context: Govern memory through its lifecycle: write only facts with a user-visible purpose and owner; read filtered by identity and tenant before ranking; use with recalled facts labeled separately; correct with update, deletion, and expiry; audit why a memory entered a turn.
variants.prompt: A user asks why the assistant “remembered” something. Put the lifecycle stages the answer depends on in order.

items.text: It was labeled as recalled memory in the turn.
It can be corrected or deleted on request.
The audit trail explains its entry into the turn.
It was read under the user’s identity filter.
It was written with a purpose and owner.

variants.hint: Audit provenance is the answer to “why”.
variants.explanation: Retain enough provenance to explain why a memory entered a particular turn.

variants.title: Govern memory
variants.context: Govern memory through its lifecycle: write only facts with a user-visible purpose and owner; read filtered by identity and tenant before ranking; use with recalled facts labeled separately; correct with update, deletion, and expiry; audit why a memory entered a turn.
variants.prompt: An assistant stores every generated token as long-term memory. Put the corrected lifecycle in order.

items.text: Audit provenance.
Correct through update, deletion, and expiry.
Read with identity and tenant filters.
Write only facts with a user-visible purpose; never secrets, credentials, or unsafe guesses.
Use recalled facts labeled separately.

variants.hint: The write policy is where this went wrong.
variants.explanation: Do not store secrets, raw tool credentials, unsafe model guesses, or every generated token.
